candidate.answerReason: Every allowed sequence reaches a rotation of the cycle \((g,g,0)\) before term 2006, where \(g=\gcd(999,a_2)\). Parity repeats every three terms, so the condition is equivalent to \(a_2\) being odd and coprime to 999. Inclusion-exclusion counts 324 such values.

methods.label: Find the eventual cycle, then use parity
methods.explanation:
The absolute-difference rule preserves common divisors and tends to make the entries smaller. These two observations identify the eventual cycle; parity then tells us which position of that cycle occurs at term \(2006\).

Let \(b=a_2\), so \(0\le b\le998\), and let \(g=\gcd(999,b)\ge1\). A number divides both \(u\) and \(v\) exactly when it divides both \(v\) and \(|v-u|\). Therefore the greatest common divisor of every consecutive pair remains \(g\).

We must also show that the repeating part begins soon enough. A pair \((u,v)\) changes to \((v,|v-u|)\). If an entry is zero or the entries are equal, the sequence repeats a rotation of
\[
t,t,0,t,t,0,\ldots.
\]
Otherwise, both entries are positive and unequal. If \(u>v\), both entries of the next pair, \((v,u-v)\), are smaller than \(u\). If \(v>u\), the next two pairs are
\[
(v,v-u),\qquad(v-u,u),
\]
and both entries of the latter are smaller than \(v\). Thus, outside the repeating part, the largest entry drops by at least \(1\) within two transitions.

The initial largest entry is \(999\). After at most \(2(999-1)=1996\) transitions, either a repeating pair has already appeared or the largest entry is \(1\), which itself forces a repeating pair. Hence the sequence is repeating by the pair \((a_{1997},a_{1998})\). The preserved greatest common divisor shows that \(t=g\), so \(a_{2006}\) is either \(0\) or \(g\). In particular, obtaining \(1\) requires \(g=1\).

To determine the phase, an absolute difference has the same parity as the sum of its inputs. Consequently, \(a_{n+3}\) has the parity of \(a_{n+2}+a_{n+1}\), which has the parity of \(a_n+2a_{n+1}\), and hence of \(a_n\). Parity therefore repeats every three terms. Since
\[
2006=3\cdot668+2,
\]
\(a_{2006}\) has the parity of \(b\). When \(g=1\), its only possible values are \(0\) and \(1\), so it equals \(1\) exactly when \(b\) is odd.

We have proved both directions: the valid starting values are exactly the odd integers from \(1\) through \(997\) that are coprime to \(999\). Since
\[
999=3^3\cdot37,
\]
we must exclude multiples of \(3\) or \(37\). There are \(499\) odd candidates. Among them, \(166\) are multiples of \(3\), corresponding to odd quotients from \(1\) through \(331\); \(13\) are multiples of \(37\), corresponding to odd quotients from \(1\) through \(25\). The \(4\) odd multiples of \(111=3\cdot37\) were excluded twice and must be added back. Thus the count is
\[
499-166-13+4=\boxed{324},
\]
choice B.

needsNewNodes.name: Termination bounds by integer descent
needsNewNodes.description: Identify a nonnegative integer quantity that decreases by at least one within a bounded number of steps outside a specified terminal class. Prove the decrease in every case and derive an explicit bound on the time to reach that class.
needsNewNodes.reason: The proof needs a uniform bound on reaching the repeating pairs. The catalog's invariant node concerns preserved quantities, while simple recurrence evaluation does not capture this bounded-descent argument.
